content: Preterm birth, defined as delivery occurring between 20 and 36 completed weeks of gestation, is a significant global cause of perinatal morbidity and mortality. Oxytocin receptor antagonists (ORA), such as atosiban, have been specifically developed to manage preterm labor. These agents are proposed as effective tocolytics, aiming to delay labor with fewer adverse effects compared to other tocolytic drugs. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of ORA on maternal, fetal, and neonatal outcomes in women experiencing preterm labor, compared to placebo or other tocolytic agents. The review included randomized controlled trials (both published and unpublished) involving women between 20 and 36 weeks of gestation. Data were extracted and analyzed independently by two reviewers, with additional information sought from trial authors when necessary. Results were presented as risk ratios (RR) for categorical data and mean differences (MD) for continuous data, with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Where applicable, the number needed to treat for benefit (NNTB) or harm (NNTH) was calculated. This updated review incorporated eight additional studies, bringing the total to 14 studies involving 2,485 women. Four studies (854 women) compared ORA (three using atosiban and one using barusiban) with placebo. Among these, three studies were deemed to have a low risk of bias, while the fourth did not adequately blind the intervention. No significant differences were observed in the rate of birth within 48 hours of trial entry (average RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.15 to 7.43; two studies, 152 women), perinatal mortality (RR 2.25, 95% CI 0.79 to 6.38; two studies, 729 infants), or major neonatal morbidity. However, ORA (atosiban) was associated with a slight reduction in birthweight (MD -138.86 g, 95% CI -250.53 to -27.18; two studies, 676 infants). In one study, atosiban was linked to an increased risk of extremely preterm birth (before 28 weeks of gestation) (RR 3.11, 95% CI 1.02 to 9.51; NNTH 31, 95% CI 8 to 3188) and infant deaths up to 12 months of age (RR 6.13, 95% CI 1.38 to 27.13; NNTH 28, 95% CI 6 to 377). However, these findings may have been confounded by the randomization of more women with pregnancies under 26 weeks of gestation to the atosiban group. ORA also resulted in an increased incidence of maternal adverse drug reactions requiring cessation of treatment compared to placebo (RR 4.02, 95% CI 2.05 to 7.85; NNTH 12, 95% CI 5 to 33). No differences were observed in preterm birth rates before 37 weeks of gestation or other adverse neonatal outcomes. Data were insufficient to determine differences between types of ORA. Eight studies (1,402 women) compared ORA (atosiban only) with betamimetics. Four of these studies were considered to have a low risk of bias. No statistically significant differences were found in the rate of birth within 48 hours of trial entry (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.22; eight studies, 1,389 women), very preterm birth (RR 1.70, 95% CI 0.89 to 3.23; one study, 145 women), extremely preterm birth (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.92; one study, 244 women), or perinatal mortality (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.21 to 1.48; three studies, 816 infants). One study (80 women) of unclear methodological quality reported an increase in the interval between trial entry and birth (MD 22.90 days, 95% CI 18.03 to 27.77). No significant differences were observed in measures of major neonatal morbidity, although the sample sizes were small. ORA (atosiban) was associated with fewer maternal adverse effects requiring cessation of treatment compared to betamimetics (RR 0.05, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.11; NNTB 6, 95% CI 6 to 6; five studies, 1,161 women). Two studies (225 women) compared ORA (atosiban) with calcium channel blockers (CCB), specifically nifedipine. Both studies were considered to have a high risk of bias due to lack of blinding, and in one study, it was unclear whether allocation was blinded. No significant differences were observed in the rate of birth within 48 hours of trial entry (average RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.44 to 2.73; two studies, 225 women) or extremely preterm birth (RR 2.14, 95% CI 0.20 to 23.11; one study, 145 women). Data on perinatal mortality were not available. One small trial (145 women) without blinding reported an increase in preterm births before 37 weeks of gestation (RR 1.56, 95% CI 1.13 to 2.14; NNTH 5, 95% CI 3 to 19), a lower gestational age at birth (MD -1.20 weeks, 95% CI -2.15 to -0.25), and an increased rate of neonatal intensive care unit admissions (RR 1.70, 95% CI 1.17 to 2.47; NNTH 5, 95% CI 3 to 20). ORA (atosiban) was associated with fewer maternal adverse effects (RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.68; NNTB 6, 95% CI 5 to 12; two studies, 225 women), but not fewer maternal adverse effects requiring cessation of treatment (RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.01 to 8.62; one study, 145 women). No long-term outcome data were included in the review. In conclusion, this review did not demonstrate the superiority of ORA (primarily atosiban) over placebo, betamimetics, or CCB (primarily nifedipine) in terms of prolonging pregnancy or improving neonatal outcomes. However, ORA was associated with fewer maternal adverse effects compared to betamimetics or CCB. The observed increase in infant deaths and extremely preterm births in one placebo-controlled study warrants caution, although the number of women enrolled at very early gestations was small. Given the limitations of small sample sizes and methodological concerns, further well-designed randomized controlled trials are necessary. Future studies should include comparisons of ORA with CCB, which have a better side-effect profile than betamimetics, and consider placebo-controlled trials. Additionally, future research should evaluate all relevant shortand long-term outcomes for both mothers and infants, as well as the associated costs.
